title: Extreme Streaming

steps.title: Text A · What the study measured
steps.html:
Written for this course, from Exelmans & Van den Bulck, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 13(8), 2017.

In 2017 two researchers at a Belgian university asked four hundred and twenty-three adults between eighteen and twenty-five how they watched television. More than four in five described themselves as binge viewers — people who watch several episodes of the same drama series back to back — and, of those, about a fifth said that they had done it at least a few times a week in the previous month. Nobody at that point had asked whether the habit did any harm, and nobody had suggested that it might.

The answer was not the obvious one. The researchers reported that binge viewers had poorer sleep quality, more fatigue and more symptoms of insomnia than other people, and that binge viewers were roughly twice as likely to sleep badly. What makes the result interesting is the comparison. Ordinary television viewing — switching between a cookery programme with its celebrity chef, a home improvement programme with its DIY tips, whatever is on — showed no such link at all. Hours in front of a screen were not the problem.

What explained the difference was arousal. The study found that the effect ran entirely through how mentally alert people were as they went to bed: the mind stayed inside the story after the screen had been turned off. The lead author explained that the more often young people binge-watched, the higher their cognitive arousal before sleep, and said that this in turn affected sleep quality, fatigue and insomnia. She was careful about the limits, adding that the study was a survey rather than an experiment, so it could not establish which came first.

steps.title: Text B · What the design does
steps.html:
Written for this course.

None of this is accidental on the producers’ side. A drama series is built with a gripping plot broken off at the worst possible moment and the next episode starting by itself, and no commercial break has ever survived contact with that design. Streaming did not invent the cliffhanger; it removed the week that used to follow it. Producers rarely deny this; one has said that the aim is simply to remove every reason to stop, and another has admitted that the design works best on tired people. When a colleague asked me what had actually changed since the days of one episode a week, the honest answer was: the pause.

There is a gap, too, between what people say they watch and what they finish. Asked what they would like more of, viewers almost always mention a current affairs programme or in-depth news, and the same viewers spend the evening with an old sitcom they have already seen twice, playing while they do something else. That is not dishonesty. It is the difference between the viewer somebody intends to be and the one who is tired at half past ten.

The authors’ own recommendation is duller than the headlines it produced. They argued that measures of media exposure ought to take account of how engaged the user is, not merely how long the screen was on, and suggested that anything which reduces arousal before bed would help more than a rule about hours. Whether a habit is addictive, in other words, may depend less on how much of it you consume than on how far into it you go — which is an uncomfortable thought, because engagement is exactly what everybody says they want from television.

Written for this course, from Exelmans & Van den Bulck, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 13(8), 2017.

In 2017 two researchers at a Belgian university asked four hundred and twenty-three adults between eighteen and twenty-five how they watched television. More than four in five described themselves as binge viewers — people who watch several episodes of the same drama series back to back — and, of those, about a fifth said that they had done it at least a few times a week in the previous month. Nobody at that point had asked whether the habit did any harm, and nobody had suggested that it might.

The answer was not the obvious one. The researchers reported that binge viewers had poorer sleep quality, more fatigue and more symptoms of insomnia than other people, and that binge viewers were roughly twice as likely to sleep badly. What makes the result interesting is the comparison. Ordinary television viewing — switching between a cookery programme with its celebrity chef, a home improvement programme with its DIY tips, whatever is on — showed no such link at all. Hours in front of a screen were not the problem.

What explained the difference was arousal. The study found that the effect ran entirely through how mentally alert people were as they went to bed: the mind stayed inside the story after the screen had been turned off. The lead author explained that the more often young people binge-watched, the higher their cognitive arousal before sleep, and said that this in turn affected sleep quality, fatigue and insomnia. She was careful about the limits, adding that the study was a survey rather than an experiment, so it could not establish which came first.

Text B · What the design does

Written for this course.

None of this is accidental on the producers’ side. A drama series is built with a gripping plot broken off at the worst possible moment and the next episode starting by itself, and no commercial break has ever survived contact with that design. Streaming did not invent the cliffhanger; it removed the week that used to follow it. Producers rarely deny this; one has said that the aim is simply to remove every reason to stop, and another has admitted that the design works best on tired people. When a colleague asked me what had actually changed since the days of one episode a week, the honest answer was: the pause.

There is a gap, too, between what people say they watch and what they finish. Asked what they would like more of, viewers almost always mention a current affairs programme or in-depth news, and the same viewers spend the evening with an old sitcom they have already seen twice, playing while they do something else. That is not dishonesty. It is the difference between the viewer somebody intends to be and the one who is tired at half past ten.

The authors’ own recommendation is duller than the headlines it produced. They argued that measures of media exposure ought to take account of how engaged the user is, not merely how long the screen was on, and suggested that anything which reduces arousal before bed would help more than a rule about hours. Whether a habit is addictive, in other words, may depend less on how much of it you consume than on how far into it you go — which is an uncomfortable thought, because engagement is exactly what everybody says they want from television.

In 2017 two researchers at a Belgian university asked four hundred and twenty-three adults between eighteen and twenty-five how they watched television. More than four in five described themselves as binge viewers — people who watch several episodes of the same drama series back to back — and, of those, about a fifth said that they had done it at least a few times a week in the previous month. Nobody at that point had asked whether the habit did any harm, and nobody had suggested that it might.

The researchers reported that binge viewers had poorer sleep quality, more fatigue and more symptoms of insomnia than other people, and that binge viewers were roughly twice as likely to sleep badly. What makes the result interesting is the comparison. Hours in front of a screen were not the problem.

What explained the difference was arousal. The study found that the effect ran entirely through how mentally alert people were as they went to bed: the mind stayed inside the story after the screen had been turned off. The lead author explained that the more often young people binge-watched, the higher their cognitive arousal before sleep, and said that this in turn affected sleep quality, fatigue and insomnia. steps.html:
Text A · What the study measured

Written for this course, from Exelmans & Van den Bulck, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine 13(8), 2017.

In 2017 two researchers at a Belgian university asked four hundred and twenty-three adults between eighteen and twenty-five how they watched television. More than four in five described themselves as binge viewers — people who watch several episodes of the same drama series back to back — and, of those, about a fifth said that they had done it at least a few times a week in the previous month. Nobody at that point had asked whether the habit did any harm, and nobody had suggested that it might.

The answer was not the obvious one. The researchers reported that binge viewers had poorer sleep quality, more fatigue and more symptoms of insomnia than other people, and that binge viewers were roughly twice as likely to sleep badly. What makes the result interesting is the comparison. Ordinary television viewing — switching between a cookery programme with its celebrity chef, a home improvement programme with its DIY tips, whatever is on — showed no such link at all. Hours in front of a screen were not the problem.

What explained the difference was arousal. The study found that the effect ran entirely through how mentally alert people were as they went to bed: the mind stayed inside the story after the screen had been turned off. The lead author explained that the more often young people binge-watched, the higher their cognitive arousal before sleep, and said that this in turn affected sleep quality, fatigue and insomnia. She was careful about the limits, adding that the study was a survey rather than an experiment, so it could not establish which came first.

Text B · What the design does

Written for this course.

None of this is accidental on the producers’ side. A drama series is built with a gripping plot broken off at the worst possible moment and the next episode starting by itself, and no commercial break has ever survived contact with that design. Streaming did not invent the cliffhanger; it removed the week that used to follow it. Producers rarely deny this; one has said that the aim is simply to remove every reason to stop, and another has admitted that the design works best on tired people. When a colleague asked me what had actually changed since the days of one episode a week, the honest answer was: the pause.

There is a gap, too, between what people say they watch and what they finish. Asked what they would like more of, viewers almost always mention a current affairs programme or in-depth news, and the same viewers spend the evening with an old sitcom they have already seen twice, playing while they do something else. That is not dishonesty. It is the difference between the viewer somebody intends to be and the one who is tired at half past ten.

The authors’ own recommendation is duller than the headlines it produced. They argued that measures of media exposure ought to take account of how engaged the user is, not merely how long the screen was on, and suggested that anything which reduces arousal before bed would help more than a rule about hours. Whether a habit is addictive, in other words, may depend less on how much of it you consume than on how far into it you go — which is an uncomfortable thought, because engagement is exactly what everybody says they want from television.

steps.title: Moving somebody's words into your own sentence
steps.html:
Statements and questions — and the four things that shift.

When you report what somebody said, four things usually shift: the tense goes back one step, the pronouns change, the time and place words change, and in questions the word order changes.

Tense. Present → past, past → past perfect, will → would, can → could. 'It is giving viewers what they want' → He said it was giving viewers what they wanted.

The shift is not compulsory. If what was said is still true, you can leave the present: She said streaming removes the schedule. Both are correct; the shifted version is more neutral.

Time and place. now → then, today → that day, yesterday → the day before, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that.

Questions. The word order becomes statement order, and the auxiliary disappears: 'Are they the same people?' → Researchers asked whether they were the same people. Never asked were they the same people. Use if or whether for yes/no questions, and keep the question word for the others: She asked what they had lost.

say and tell are not interchangeable. Tell needs a person: He told me it was fine. Say does not take one: He said it was fine, or He said to me…

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences from the two texts.

The head of the company said it was giving viewers what they already wanted.
Present → past.

Critics replied that it was manufacturing a habit.
Reply that — no person needed.

Six in ten adults say they binge-watch.
No shift: still true.

Most of them describe it as relaxing.
Describe as, not describe that.

A smaller number report feeling worse afterwards.
Report + -ing.

Researchers asked whether those were the same people.
Yes/no question → whether, statement order.

Somebody admitted that they had tested the countdown at fifteen seconds.
Past → past perfect.

My grandmother could tell you what was on at eight.
Tell takes a person.

A programme could assume its audience had seen the news.
Past perfect for the earlier viewing.

When asked what they had lost, viewers said almost nothing.
Reduced passive: when they were asked.

Asked separately what they missed, a third mentioned it.
Same reduction, participle clause.

A third of the same group mentioned watching things together.
Mention + -ing.

steps.title: Reporting a question in three steps
steps.html:
1. The original: 'Do you feel worse afterwards?' asked the researcher.
  2. Step one: choose the reporting verb and the person. The researcher asked me…
  3. Step two: it is a yes/no question, so add if or whether, and put the words into statement order. The auxiliary do disappears: …whether I felt worse afterwards.
  4. Step three: shift the tense. feel → felt. Result: The researcher asked me whether I felt worse afterwards.
  5. Now a wh- question: 'What have you lost?' The question word stays, the order changes, the tense shifts: She asked them what they had lost. Never what had they lost in a reported question.

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Report at least three things other people have said, using at least one reported question.
steps.html:
• Open by reporting something somebody used to say.
  • Report a second person, using <i>told me</i> or <i>said that</i>.
  • Report at least one question, in statement order.
  • Close with what you do now.

Useful language

  • My mother always said that …
  • A friend of mine told me that …
  • When I asked her what she missed, she said …
  • She asked me whether I …
  • The company claimed it was … ; critics replied that …
  • Nobody expected to miss …
steps.modelHtml:
Four in a row, and then Sunday

My father used to say that television was something you turned on at a particular time and off again afterwards. He told me once that the point of a programme was that it ended.

I did not understand this until last winter, when I watched four episodes of the same series in one evening and could not remember, the next morning, what had happened in which.

When I mentioned it to a friend, she asked me whether I had enjoyed it. I said I had, and that was true. She then asked what I would have done with those five hours otherwise, and I could not answer, which she said was exactly the point.

Now I watch one and stop. It is a small rule and I break it about once a month.
